summary: Describes steps an implementation can take between receiving user input and handing permitted code points to the IDNA2008 protocol, since IDNA2008 itself assumes input is already from a permitted set. It is informational.

eli5.summary: If you type a name with capital letters or odd characters, something has to tidy it up before it goes out. This describes how to do that tidying.

questions: how to normalize user input for idna
how to normalize domain names for idna
full width half width characters idna
subtitle: How to normalize user-typed domain names before they reach the IDNA2008 protocol.

tldr.problem: IDNA2008 expects input that has already been validated and normalized, but it does not specify how to convert what users actually type (capitals, full-width characters, decomposed accents) into that permitted form. Different applications need different mapping rules.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC describes a four-step baseline mapping: convert uppercase to lowercase, decompose full-width and half-width characters, normalize combining characters (NFC), and optionally map ideographic full stops to ASCII periods.
tldr.outcome: Applications can implement predictable, user-friendly input processing that works across different platforms, though they should customize the mapping for their specific users rather than adopt this baseline unchanged.

today: RFC 5895 is Informational and has not been updated or obsoleted. It remains the reference for user interface mapping in IDNA2008 implementations, though applications are encouraged to adapt the mapping to their specific user communities.

sections.title: Introduction and Scope
sections.content:
The IDNA2008 protocol defines how domain names with international characters are encoded and validated, but it assumes the input is already in a permitted form. This RFC addresses what happens before the protocol: user interface processing. When a user types or pastes a domain name, applications need to convert it into a form IDNA2008 can handle.

The RFC emphasizes that there is no universal mapping. Different applications need different rules depending on locale, input method (keyboard, voice, copy-paste), and user expectations. A Turkish user's "I" lowercases differently than an English user's. This document provides a baseline mapping suitable for typical hand-typed input worldwide, but applications should adapt it to their specific users.
sections.eli5: Different languages and input methods need different rules. The RFC gives a starting point, but applications should change it based on who is using them.

sections.title: The Division Between User Interface and Protocol
sections.content:
The original IDNA (IDNA2003) mixed user interface processing into the protocol itself, making implementers' lives simpler but resulting in surprising behavior for users. IDNA2008 separates these concerns: the protocol part (RFCs 5890-5893) defines validation and encoding; this RFC defines the user interface mapping part that comes before the protocol.

A user interface for international domain names is complex. It must consider the user's language, the input device, how the computer interprets the input, and how to normalize that input into Unicode characters recognizable by the DNS. A capital "I" in Turkish lowercases to U+0131 (dotless i), not U+0069 (regular i). Simple context-free rules cannot capture all these nuances, but a sensible baseline can handle most cases.
sections.eli5: IDNA2008 handles the protocol part ('now it's a valid name'). This RFC handles the user part ('I typed this, clean it up').

sections.title: The Four-Step Mapping Algorithm
sections.content:
The RFC defines four steps, applied in order, to map user input to IDNA2008-compatible code points:

Step 1: Lowercase. Convert uppercase Unicode characters to their lowercase equivalents using the Unicode Lowercase_Mapping property. This matches ASCII domain name behavior and makes things simpler for users who capitalize inconsistently.

Step 2: Decompose full-width and half-width characters. Asian input methods often produce full-width versions of Latin characters (e.g., the full-width Latin 'A', U+FF21) instead of the normal ASCII 'A'. This step converts those using the Unicode decomposition mapping.

Step 3: Apply Unicode Normalization Form C (NFC). NFC composes combining characters (like accents) into single precomposed characters. Users may type an 'e' followed by an accent mark, but IDNA2008 requires the precomposed 'é'. NFC handles this automatically.

Step 4: Map ideographic full stops. The ideographic full stop (U+3002, a dot used in CJK text) can be mapped to the ASCII period (U+002E) for label separation, since some input methods do not easily produce the ASCII period.
sections.eli5: Step 1: Make capitals small. Step 2: Convert weird 'A' to regular A. Step 3: Combine accent marks with letters. Step 4: Turn the fancy dot into a regular dot. That's the order to do it in.

sections.title: Implementing Sensible Mapping
sections.content:
The RFC includes a strong caveat: if you are implementing this four-step algorithm exactly, you are probably doing it wrong. The authors recommend that implementers read the introduction section carefully and think about their specific users before adopting this baseline unchanged.

Good mappings for the real world might differ significantly based on assumptions about how users think or type. For example, a mapping for spoken input (speech-to-text) would be very different from one for typed input. A mapping for users copy-pasting from documents might be different from one for users typing manually. The baseline is a starting point, not a finished product.

Useful modifications might include handling Pinyin (romanized Chinese input), applying context-aware case folding for specific languages, or adjusting the mapping based on the domain's registered scripts.
sections.eli5: The four steps are a template, not a final answer. Think about your actual users and change the steps if needed.

sections.title: Security and Character Confusion
sections.content:
The RFC notes that mappings can cause confusion for users. Converting uppercase to lowercase, for example, might result in homoglyphs: different characters that look the same after normalization. A capital and lowercase version of a letter might look identical on screen, confusing users about which domain they registered or are accessing.

Security concerns about character confusion are not fully addressed in this RFC or the other IDNA2008 documents. Implementers and administrators should be aware that normalization can create unexpected equivalences and design user interfaces to mitigate confusion where possible.
sections.eli5: When characters look too similar after normalization, users might get confused about which domain is which. Be careful about that.
